ds_context: The Substation Electrical Transformer Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) highlights several critical components that can fail and impact the overall transformer performance. The Winding Insulation (INS-01) is prone to insulation failure due to overheating, ageing, and voltage stress, leading to thermal degradation, electrical treeing, and corona effects. The Active Part (ACT-01) can experience overexcitation from voltage overload, frequency overload, or stray loss, causing iron loss, copper loss, and increased risk of insulation failure. The Cooling System (CLG-01) can leak due to ageing, corrosion, or vibration, resulting in liquid evaporation, pipe erosion, and gasket deterioration. The Buchholz Relay (BRC-01) may fail to operate because of dirt accumulation, insect infestation, or mechanical wear, leading to electrical contact failure. The Pressure Relief Valve (PRV-01) can fail to relieve pressure due to ageing, corrosion, or overpressure, causing metal fatigue, erosion, and deposit buildup. The Conservator (CVS-01) can leak from ageing, corrosion, or overpressure, leading to liquid evaporation, pipe erosion, and gasket deterioration. The Tap Changer (TCT-01) can fail to change taps due to dirt accumulation, wear and tear, or lubrication failure, resulting in mechanical wear, electrical contact failure, and lubrication failure. The Breather (BTH-01) can fail to regulate pressure due to dirt accumulation, moisture ingress, or mechanical wear, leading to diaphragm failure and valve sticking. The Excitation System (EXC-01) can fail to regulate voltage due to ageing, corrosion, or overvoltage, causing insulation failure and reduced transformer lifespan. The severity of these failure modes is high, but the ability to detect degradation is moderate to high, emphasizing the need for regular maintenance and monitoring to predict and prevent failures.
question_context: To build an effective anomaly model for substation electrical transformers, it is crucial to consider specific environmental factors, such as temperature, humidity, and altitude, that can affect performance. Key performance indicators (KPIs) like temperature, pressure, and vibration can be used to measure the health of the asset, with known failure modes like overheating, leakage, and insulation failure being the focus of the anomaly model's design. Data quality issues, such as missing values, outliers, and noise, are commonly encountered in sensor data and should be addressed. Performance metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score can be used to evaluate the model's performance. The expected outcomes of the anomaly model include alerts, notifications, or reports, which should be communicated to relevant stakeholders. The anomaly model can be used for predictive maintenance, real-time monitoring, or condition-based monitoring, with Python, R, or specific machine learning libraries being potential tools for building the model. Failures can progress from an initial anomalous state to a complete failure over time, and specific threshold values for KPIs can indicate an anomalous state. Data privacy, security, regulatory, and compliance requirements must be considered, as well as computational or resource constraints. Sensor data is collected at a specific frequency and sampling rate, and critical components and failure modes beyond those listed in the FMEA summary should be considered. The detection of Active Part (ACT-01) failures, Tap Changer (TCT-01) wear and tear, Excitation System (EXC-01) degradation, Pressure Relief Valve (PRV-01) pressure thresholds, Conservator (CVS-01) leakage, Winding Insulation (INS-01) overheating, ageing, and voltage stress, Breather (BTH-01) failure, Cooling System (CLG-01) leaks, and Buchholz Relay (BRC-01) failure are all critical for predicting and preventing failures.
